title: Latency-aware path selection and mTLS degradation plan
content:
Purpose:
This note collects ideas and a concrete plan for making path selection sensitive to observed latency/SLO budgets while allowing a controlled, auditable degradation of mTLS enforcement in extreme failure scenarios. It is intended to bridge platform-level routing policy with SRE runbooks and to give the control plane clear heuristics for automated fallback.

Context / motivation:
- We have several inter-region and intra-region handoffs where strict mTLS + L7 policy checks cause request failures when sidecars or certificate rotation lags occur.
- Customers require both: 1) hard failure guarantees for sensitive tenants, 2) best-effort low-latency routing for public-hosted workloads.
- Current fallback is binary (reject or accept) and driven by single-instance health checks. This leads to cascading failures and unacceptably high tail latency when control-plane calls to the cert manager or CA are delayed.

High-level goals:
- Make routing decisions aware of the application-level latency budget (per-route SLO) and choose path that optimizes for latency while maintaining highest reasonable security posture.
- Define an explicit, auditable mTLS degradation state machine with telemetry and TTLs to avoid indefinite insecure modes.
- Keep control-plane logic simple and deterministic; prefer rule-based policies over opaque ML decisions for now.
- Ensure operator-visible signals (dashboards + alerts) when a route transitions into a degraded mTLS state.

Key terms / invariants:
- Path: a specific route through edge -> regional-proxy -> service-cluster.
- SLO budget: configured p99 latency for a route (e.g., 150ms).
- Degradation window: short TTL during which mTLS checks can be relaxed for a route (default 3 minutes).
- Enforcement tiers: strict, permissive, bypass.
  - strict: mTLS required, L7 policy enforced at ingress.
  - permissive: mTLS attempted but fallback to plaintext allowed if TLS handshake/validation fails. L7 policy still applies where possible.
  - bypass: upstream-only acceptance; mTLS not required on this path (only used for emergency heat).

Decision heuristics (control plane):
1) Monitor per-path latency and error rate (p50/p95/p99, client-side TLS handshake errors, RSTs) and cert-manager latency for signing/rotation.
2) If p99 > SLO threshold AND upstream cost (measured as additional ms added by verification/sidecar) > X ms for 3 consecutive windows -> consider degrading enforcement one tier down.
3) Before applying degradation, check tenant policy: if tenant has security_override=deny_degrade then abort and page SRE.
4) When degrading, write an auditable event with reason, affected routes, TTL, and operator (auto or user) into the control-plane event log. Emit metrics: route.degradation{route,reason,tier}.
5) Apply network config change only at edge or regional-proxy layer — prefer making the least-scoped change (edge->regional link) rather than cluster-wide unless root cause is cluster-local.
6) Re-evaluate every 30s; if metrics return to acceptable range for two consecutive windows, promote back to strict.

Operational constraints and safety guards:
- Max consecutive auto-degrades per route per 24h = 3. After that, switch to manual review.
- Degradations cannot escalate from permissive to bypass without at least one manual acknowledge by an SRE on call.
- Degradation TTLs auto-expire; a human must explicitly extend beyond 15 minutes.
- All degradations populate an incident-folder automatically and send to #platform-routing slack with a summary and links.

L4 vs L7 considerations:
- L4-level fallbacks (route around by switching regional egress or changing BGP/anycast endpoint) are faster but coarse. Use L4 when whole-region fabric shows increased latency and certificate checks are healthy.
- L7-level fallbacks (relaxing policy in sidecar or proxy) allow policy-driven routing to stay intact but require more control-plane coordination and will be slower. Use L7 fallback when the failure vector is TLS handshake or sidecar resource saturation.
- Combine: prefer L7 permissive first for tenant-routed traffic; for public low-SLA routes we may do an L4 redirect to a lower-latency region without changing mTLS state.

Multi-region routing policy snippets (proposal):
- route-policy: latency-aware (preferred-region, fallback-regions[], max-additional-latency-ms)
- If local-region p99 <= max-additional-latency: stay local (strict mTLS)
- Else if fallback region p99 + network-RTT <= SLO: re-route to fallback region (maintain strict mTLS if certs present; otherwise permissive and log)
- Geo-affinity: for stateful tenants, prefer sticky routes; only allow cross-region redirect if sticky window > X and tenant consents.

Telemetry and dashboards (must-haves):
- route.latency.{p50,p95,p99} by route, region, cluster
- route.tls_handshake_errors by route and sidecar image version
- controlplane.cert_rotation_latency by cluster and CA
- route.degradation.events with reason and TTL
- a derived metric: route.slo_violation_pressure = (p99 - SLO) / SLO

Testing plan & simulation:
- Chaos experiments: inject TLS handshake latency at sidecar (delays at CA) and verify automated path decision leads to permissive with proper logging and TTL. Use chaos-lab job: PLT-CHAOS-162.
- Canary rollout: implement feature flags to enable auto-degrade for a small set of dev routes first (10 routes). Validate no tenant loses strict requirements.
- Load-test: create synthetic client traffic reproducing 99th percentile scenarios and ensure decision logic triggers within expected windows.

Runbook excerpt (for on-call):
- P1: Route enters bypass without manual ack -> page SRE immediately and run escalation.
- P2: Route in permissive for >15m -> auto-open ticket in Incident Tracker; on-call inspects cert-manager (logs: cm-rotate), sidecar health, and control-plane mem usage.
- Diagnostic checklist:
  1) Check route.degradation.events and reason.
  2) Check CA / cert-manager latency (controlplane.cert_rotation_latency).
  3) Inspect sidecar logs for TLS error types (expired cert / unknown CA / handshake timeout).
  4) If issue is cert-manager backlog, attempt rotate-cert job (gitHub runbook: github.com/redwood-inference/infra-actions/actions/rotate-cert).
  5) If traffic pressure seems to cause sidecar OOM, scale sidecar resources or apply temporary L4 redirect to alternate region.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- How to encode tenant-level opt-outs without creating an explosion of special-case policy rules? Propose a tiered policy template and inheritance model.
- Is the 3-minute default TTL reasonable? We need experiments to determine median recovery time for common failure modes.
- Should we implement a control-plane dry-run mode to simulate degraded states and verify metric triggers before actual config changes? (I vote yes.)

Next steps / TODOs:
- [ ] Draft control-plane PR with state machine + event schema (owner: @ElenaRossi, JIRA: JIRA-PLT-892).
- [ ] Implement dashboard for route.degradation.events (owner: @TomBaker).
- [ ] Add test harness in chaos-lab and schedule two experiments (owner: @Samir).
- [ ] Run canary on 10 low-sensitivity routes for 48h (owner: platform-eng oncall).

Notes to self / informal bits:
- Prefer simple TTL-based safety rather than trying to auto-optimize TTLs; humans can iterate after we have data.
- Keep the audit log readable (JSON events ok, but include short human summary).
- Expect product questions about how this influences compliance — include a short FAQ for security team once draft is stable.

References / links:
- Confluence design: CONFLUENCE-PLATFORM-1452 (draft)
- Related PR: github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/418
- Incident where current fallback caused p99 spike: incident-2025-06-11-route-throttle (internal)

End.
